title: Your study

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' one-line prayer for his sister: heal her now. Your prayer. Now the words you read, and keep reading.

People say "my song" about a track they've played so often it feels like theirs. Psalm 1 does something like that, and at first it looks like a slip. The verse starts with "the law of the LORD." A few words later, in the Hebrew, it's torato: his Torah. Whose? God's, or the reader's?
screen: `"MY SONG."` → `THE LAW OF THE LORD.` → `THEN: HIS TORAH. WHOSE?`

segments.voice: Here's the line in the JPS translation: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in His law doth he meditate day and night." The translators capitalized that second His, reading it as God's. That's a fair reading. The Talmud hears something else in the Hebrew. At first, it says, the Torah is called the LORD's. After a person has labored over it, it's called his own. So the puzzle is the point: the text starts out belonging to God, and with enough study, it also belongs to you. Pirkei Avot has a sage with an unusual name, Ben Bag Bag, who says: turn it, and turn it, for everything is in it. That's how a text becomes yours. Not by reading it once, but by coming back. A psalm. A chapter of Avot. This week's portion. A page of Talmud with a study partner on the phone. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud reads Psalm 1 as saying the Torah becomes the student's own.

segments.voice: Open your text, on paper or a screen, to a line you already know. Read it slowly three times. On the third time, look for one word you'd never noticed before, and stay with that word.
screen: `A LINE YOU KNOW.` · `READ IT THREE TIMES.` · `ONE NEW WORD.`

segments.voice: Your study: the text you keep coming back to, turned so often it becomes yours, as the Talmud reads Psalm 1.
Your line: your text, turned so often that it has turned you a little. Shalom, friend.
